q: Which of the following is NOT one of the purposes of a paper-based medical record listed in the lecture?
explanation: The lecture lists five purposes: recall observations, inform others, gain knowledge, monitor performance, and justify interventions. Automated alerts are an EHR/CDSS function.

q: Analyzing medical records to understand disease patterns and identify adverse drug reactions corresponds to which purpose of the medical record?
explanation: 'Gain knowledge' is described as analyzing records to aid research, understand disease patterns, and identify adverse drug reactions.

q: Tracking the effectiveness of drug therapies, following up on lab results, and understanding disease progression is which purpose of the medical record?
explanation: The lecture defines 'monitor performance' as tracking drug therapy effectiveness, lab follow-up, and disease progression.

q: The inability of paper records to include MRI or other radiology images illustrates which problem of paper records?
explanation: The lecture lists three problems of paper records: limited access, huge storage space, and lack of multimedia information such as radiology images (MRI).

q: According to the lecture's definition of an EHR, what is its scope?
options: Limited to a single physician's office
Used only by the patient on a mobile app
Restricted to a single inpatient ward
explanation: The EHR is defined as a digital record shared across departments, with a scope spanning different healthcare organizations.

q: The term 'EHR system' differs from 'EHR' mainly because the system also includes:
options: A scanned archive of the original paper charts kept for legal reasons
The insurer's claims forms and billing records
The patient's full genome sequence and biobank samples
Active tools to manage information, e.g., decision support
explanation: The EHR system includes the active tools used to manage information (e.g., visualization, decision support); the two terms are often used interchangeably.

q: In the example EHR, entries such as '250: Diabetes' and '401.9: Hypertension' represent which data type?
explanation: The lecture shows four EHR data types (images/videos, bio-signals, free text, coded data); ICD codes like 250 and 401.9 are coded data.

q: Which of the following is listed in the lecture as a DISADVANTAGE of EHR compared with paper records?
options: Serving multiple users and uses at the same time
Initial investment in hardware, software, and training
explanation: Disadvantages listed are initial investment, time to learn, and system failures/security; the other options are advantages.

q: In the case study of a southern Taiwan medical center (~1,400 beds) that abolished paper records, what were the estimated annual savings in costs and labor?
explanation: The case study reports annual savings of about 8M NTD; 2.2M NTD was the reduced paper/printing cost.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five functional components of an EHR system presented in the lecture?
explanation: The five components are patient data capture and review, CPOE, CDSS, access to knowledge resources, and integrated communication and reporting support.

q: Which coding standard is used for medical imaging in the lecture's block diagram of multiple-source-data systems?
explanation: The block diagram maps imaging to DICOM, laboratory to LOINC, medication to RxNorm/ATC, and clinical terms to SNOMED CT.

q: In 'ICD-10-CM', what does 'CM' stand for?
explanation: ICD-10-CM is the International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision, Clinical Modification, used for diagnoses.

q: Which of the following is NOT a use of the ATC code in EHRs mentioned in the lecture?
options: Standardized medication coding across hospitals and countries
Supporting CDSS such as drug-drug interaction checks
explanation: ATC (Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical) codes medications; laboratory observations are coded with LOINC.

q: The lecture shows many different expressions for 'myocardial infarction' (心肌梗塞). Which standard addresses this by providing a common clinical language for indexing, storing, retrieving and aggregating data?
explanation: SNOMED CT is a standardized terminology providing a common language that handles variations in clinical expressions.

q: Which standard describes data formats and elements called 'resources' together with an API for exchanging EHRs?
explanation: FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) defines resources and an API for EHR exchange; CDA is a document markup standard.

q: HL7 CDA (Clinical Document Architecture) is a document markup standard belonging to which HL7 version?
explanation: The lecture describes HL7 Version 3 CDA as specifying the structure and semantics of clinical documents for exchange.

q: In a clinical note following the SOAP format, what does the 'A' stand for?
explanation: SOAP stands for Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan.

q: The phenomenon in which clinicians become desensitized to frequent CDSS warnings and override most drug alerts is called:
explanation: The lecture discusses high overridden rates of drug alerts (often over 50%) and names this alert fatigue (警示疲乏).

q: Taiwan's NHI PharmaCloud system allows physicians and pharmacists to check a patient's outpatient and inpatient prescription records for what period?
explanation: PharmaCloud, an example of electronic interface data capture, shows prescription records from the preceding 3 months.

q: A data entry system flags a record of prostate cancer in a female patient. Which type of data validation is this?
explanation: The lecture gives 'prostate cancer in female' as the example of a consistency check.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three data display methods presented in the lecture?
explanation: The three data display methods are timeline graphs, timeline flowsheets, and summaries and snapshots.

q: Using the EHR to identify patients who are receiving a recalled drug such as rofecoxib (Vioxx) falls under which query and surveillance category?
explanation: Under clinical care, the lecture lists encouraging preventive care and identifying patients receiving a recalled drug (side effects, product quality).

q: Why was rofecoxib (Vioxx) withdrawn from the market in 2004?
options: Increased risk of heart attacks and strokes
Severe liver toxicity in elderly users
Lack of efficacy for arthritis pain
explanation: The lecture notes Vioxx, an NSAID for arthritis, was linked to nearly 28,000 heart attacks and was withdrawn by Merck in 2004.

q: Which HIMSS EMRAM stage, achieved by three Taiwanese hospitals in the lecture, represents the highest level of EMR adoption?
explanation: The lecture shows that 3 hospitals passed HIMSS EMRAM Stage 7, the highest stage.

q: Laboratory results are coded using ____ (Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes).
explanation: The lecture lists LOINC as the code standard for laboratory and clinical observations.

q: Diseases/diagnoses in the EHR are coded using the ____ code set.
explanation: The lecture adopts ICD-10-CM for disease coding.

q: Medications can be coded with RxNorm or the ____ classification system.
explanation: The lecture names RxNorm or the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) code for medications.

q: In transcription, an ____ system reads handwritten numbers, check boxes and bar codes on a paper form and passes the content to the EHR.
explanation: The lecture's transcription example uses Optical Character Recognition (OCR).

q: A serum potassium value of 50 (normal 3.5-5) entered into the EHR would be caught by a ____ check.
explanation: The lecture gives serum potassium 50 as the example of a range check.

q: CPOE stands for Computerized ____ Order Entry.
explanation: CPOE is computerized provider (physician) order entry, used for orders such as radiology, chemotherapy and TPN.

q: A record that patients themselves manage through mobile or web apps, e.g. storing their own MRIs and X-rays, is called a ____.
explanation: The lecture shows PHR mobile/web apps as an example of patient-held records.

q: Taiwan's NHI system that lets people download or print their latest treatment records, allergy, lab and immunization data is called ____.
explanation: My Health Bank empowers people to manage their health by providing treatment records and preventive health information.

q: The ____ is the executive role that bridges clinicians' information needs and IT, addressing the 'Users' Information Needs / Leadership' challenge.
explanation: The lecture names the CMIO (Chief Medical Information Officer) under the leadership challenge.

q: MIMIC, a database used for retrospective real-world studies, stands for Medical Information Mart for ____.
explanation: The lecture lists MIMIC (Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care), Taiwan NHI database and TMUCDR as real-world data sources.

q: Name the five purposes of a paper-based medical record.
answer:
1. Recall observations
2. Inform others
3. Gain knowledge
4. Monitor performance
5. Justify interventions
explanation: Slides 'Purpose of Paper-based Medical Record' at the start of the lecture.

q: Name three advantages of an EHR compared with paper-based records.
answer:
1. Comprehensiveness of information (phenotype, behavior, genotype)
2. Longer duration of use and retention of data
3. Greater degree of data structure
4. Serves multiple uses at the same time
explanation: Slide 'Recap: EHR VS Paper-based' (advantages); any three are enough.

q: Name the five functional components of an EHR system.
answer:
1. Patient data capture and review
2. Computerized provider order entry (CPOE)
3. Clinical decision support system (CDSS)
4. Access to knowledge resources
5. Integrated communication and reporting support
explanation: Section II 'Functional Components of an Electronic Health Record System'.

q: Which code standard does an EHR use for each of these data types: diseases, medications, laboratory tests, and images?
answer:
Diseases: ICD-10-CM
Medications: RxNorm or ATC
Laboratory tests: LOINC
Images: DICOM
explanation: Slides 'Adopt code standards' and the multiple-source-data block diagram.

q: Name the two general ways data are captured into an EHR.
answer:
1. Electronic interfaces from systems that are already automated (e.g., laboratory systems, PharmaCloud)
2. Direct manual data entry when no electronic source exists or it cannot be accessed
explanation: Section III 'Fundamental Issues', slide 'Data Capture'.

q: Name the four uses of EHR query and surveillance systems.
answer:
1. Clinical care
2. Clinical trials
3. Quality reporting
4. Retrospective studies
explanation: Section IV 'Query and Surveillance Systems'.

q: Name three disadvantages of an EHR compared with paper-based records.
answer:
1. Initial investment (hardware, software, training, support)
2. Takes time to learn
3. System failures
4. Security risks
explanation: Slide 'Recap: EHR VS Paper-based' (disadvantages).

q: Name three of the five challenges ahead for EHRs identified in the lecture.
answer:
1. Users' information needs / leadership
2. Usability
3. Standards
4. Privacy and security
5. Costs and benefits
explanation: Section V 'Challenges Ahead'; any three are enough.

q: Name three types of data validation checks used when entering data into an EHR.
answer:
1. Range checks (e.g., serum potassium 3.5-5)
2. Pattern checks (e.g., telephone number)
3. Consistency checks (e.g., prostate cancer in a female)
4. Spelling checks
explanation: Slide 'Data Validation' in the Data Capture section.

q: Name three problems of paper-based medical records that the EHR addresses.
answer:
Limited access: only in one place, used by one person at a time
Require huge storage space (medical records room)
Lack multimedia information such as MRI/radiology images
explanation: Slides 'Problem of Paper record' list limited access, huge space and lack of multimedia.

q: Which of the following is listed in the lecture as an ADVANTAGE of an EHR over paper-based records?
options: Lower initial investment in hardware and training
Serving multiple uses at the same time
No time needed to learn the new system
Freedom from system failures and security risks
explanation: The recap lists 'serve multiple uses at the same time' as an advantage; cost, learning time and failures/security are disadvantages.

q: Define an electronic health record (EHR) as presented in the lecture.
answer:
A digital medical record that can be shared across departments
Used across different healthcare organizations
Holds comprehensive health information: history, allergies, immunizations, labs, radiology images
explanation: Slide 'What is an Electronic Health Record (EHR)?' gives definition, scope, function and focus.

q: According to the lecture's EHR definition slide, what is the 'focus' of an EHR?
options: Billing and insurance claims for a single clinic
Patient-managed storage of personal fitness data
Comprehensive health management by different healthcare professionals
Archiving radiology images for one department
explanation: The EHR's focus is comprehensive health management from different healthcare professionals.

q: Compared with an EHR, an 'EHR system' also includes the active ____ used to manage the information, such as visualization and decision support.
explanation: The term EHR system includes the active tools (visualization, decision support) used to manage the information.

q: Name the four types of data shown in the lecture's example of an electronic health record.
answer:
Images/videos
Bio-signals
Free text
Coded data (e.g., 250: Diabetes)
explanation: The 'Example of an electronic health record' slide labels images/videos, bio-signals, free text and coded data.

q: Which EHR data type most needs natural language processing (NLP) before it can be used as structured data?
options: Coded diagnoses such as ICD codes
explanation: The recap lists 'degree of structure of data (NLP for free text)', since free text is unstructured.

q: Which of the following is NOT listed in the lecture as an input saved to the medical record?
explanation: Inputs to the medical record are personal information, lab results, treatment, nurse care, disease and medication.

q: In the southern Taiwan medical center case study, about how many staff positions could be downsized by no longer printing, storing and sending paper records?
explanation: About 25,000 person-hours saved per year converts to roughly 13 staff.

q: Describe the benefits reported when a ~1,400-bed southern Taiwan medical center abolished paper records.
answer:
Paper and printing costs reduced by about NT$2.2M
About 25,000 person-hours saved per year (~13 staff)
Clinic nursing staff save 18 hours (2.25 people)
Total savings about NT$8M per year
explanation: Slide 'Benefit - A case study from medical center'.

q: The EHR advantage 'duration of use and ____ of data' means health data can be kept and used over the long term.
explanation: The recap lists 'duration of use and retention of data' among EHR advantages.
